**Optical (photoluminescence) gap of monolayer MoS₂**

| Source | Gap value | Temperature | Notes |
|--------|-----------|-------------|-------|
| **Room‑temperature PL experiment** (e.g., Wang *et al.*, Nat. Nanotechnol. 2012; Mak *et al.*, Phys. Rev. Lett. 2010) | **≈ 1.80 eV** | 300 K | Peak at the A exciton (~1.8 eV). |
| **Low‑temperature PL (∼10 K)** | **≈ 1.84–1.86 eV** | 10 K | Slight blue shift due to reduced phonon broadening. |
| **Time‑resolved PL / exciton binding energy subtraction** | **≈ 1.82 eV** | 300 K | After accounting for ~0.5 eV exciton binding, the single‑particle band gap is ∼2.3 eV. |
| **DFT (PBE) + GW + Bethe–Salpeter Equation** | **≈ 1.80 eV** | 0 K | Theoretical optical gap matches experiment; quasiparticle gap ~2.7 eV, exciton binding ≈0.9 eV. |
| **Hybrid functional (HSE06) + BSE** | **≈ 1.78–1.82 eV** | 0 K | Consistent with GW/BSE results. |

**Summary**

The optical gap measured by photoluminescence for a monolayer of MoS₂ is about **1.80 eV at room temperature**, increasing to ~1.84–1.86 eV when cooled to cryogenic temperatures. This value corresponds to the energy of the A exciton transition and agrees well with many-body perturbation theory (GW+BSE) calculations that include strong Coulomb binding (~0.8–0.9 eV).

Die optische Bandlücke einer monolayer‑WS₂ beträgt etwa **2 eV** (≈ 1.95–2.05 eV, je nach Messmethode).  

- **Experimentell** (Photolumineszenz, Absorption): 1.95 ± 0,02 eV bei Raumtemperatur.  
- **DFT‑PBE** (Bandstruktur ohne Spin‑Orbit‑Coupling) liefert ~1.6 eV – also deutlich zu niedrig.  
- **HSE06 / GW** korrigiert die Lücke auf ≈ 2.0–2.1 eV, was mit den experimentellen Werten übereinstimmt.

Somit ist der optische Bandgap einer monolayer‑WS₂ in der Regel ~2 eV.

**Optical band‑gap of monolayer WSe₂**

| Source | Method / Technique | Optical band‑gap (E₀) |
|--------|--------------------|-----------------------|
| **Photoluminescence (PL)** | Low‑temperature (4 K) PL on exfoliated or CVD monolayers | ≈ 1.65 eV |
| **Absorption / Reflectance contrast** | Near‑normal incidence, 300–600 nm range | ≈ 1.63–1.66 eV |
| **Two‑photon absorption (TPA)** | Nonlinear optical spectroscopy | ≈ 1.62 eV |
| **DFT + GW/BSE** | Many‑body perturbation theory, G₀W₀ + Bethe–Salpeter equation | 1.60–1.70 eV (depends on substrate screening) |
| **Experiment – time‑resolved PL / TRPL** | Exciton lifetime studies | Consistent with ≈ 1.65 eV transition energy |

**Key points**

- The optical gap corresponds to the A exciton resonance in monolayer WSe₂.
- Slight variations (±0.02 eV) arise from temperature, dielectric environment (substrate or encapsulation), and sample quality.
- At room temperature the PL peak shifts down by ~30–40 meV compared with 4 K, giving a typical value of **≈ 1.60 eV**.

So, for most practical purposes, the optical band‑gap of monolayer WSe₂ is taken as **~1.65 eV (low temperature)** or **~1.60 eV (room temperature)**.

In the simplest π‑band tight‑binding description of monolayer graphene, only the nearest‑neighbour hopping between adjacent \(p_z\) orbitals is retained.  
The hopping integral \(t\) (sometimes denoted \(\gamma_0\)) is found to be

\[
t \;\approx\; 2.7~\text{eV}
\]

This value is obtained from:

| Source | Method / Reference |
|--------|--------------------|
| **DFT** (PBE‑GGA) band‑structure fitting | \(t = 2.71~\text{eV}\) (e.g., S. Reich *et al.*, PRB 2002) |
| **HSE06 hybrid functional** | \(t \approx 2.75~\text{eV}\) |
| **Experiment** (ARPES, optical conductivity) | \(t = 2.7–2.8~\text{eV}\) |

Thus, the nearest‑neighbour hopping used in most tight‑binding models of graphene is about **\(2.7\,\text{eV}\)**.

Die Messungen zeigen, dass die Curie‑Temperatur (Tc) der monokristallinen Schicht von **CrI₃** etwa **45 K** beträgt (≈ −228 °C). Diese Zahl stammt aus experimentellen Magneto‑Raman- und SQUID‑Messungen bei niedrigen Temperaturen. In theoretischen Berechnungen (z. B. DFT‑PBE mit Spin‑Orbit‑Coupling und Monte‑Carlo‑Simulationen) liegt Tc typischerweise etwas höher, im Bereich von 50–60 K, was die experimentelle Beobachtung bestätigt.

Monolayer **CrI₃** is a two‑dimensional ferromagnet with the magnetic moments aligned perpendicular to the plane (out‑of‑plane or “c‑axis” direction).  The Cr³⁺ ions carry a local moment of ≈ 3 µ_B, and the exchange coupling between nearest‑neighbor Cr atoms is strongly ferromagnetic.  Consequently, at low temperatures the monolayer orders in a **ferromagnetic (FM) phase** with all spins pointing either up or down along the crystallographic c‑axis.

**Xenes that have been theoretically predicted to host a quantum‑spin‑Hall (QSH) insulating state**

| Xene | Predicted bulk band gap (Δ) | Method / Reference |
|------|-----------------------------|--------------------|
| **Silicene** | ≈ 1.5 meV (≈ 17 K) | DFT–PBE + SOC (e.g., Liu *et al.*, PRL 2011) |
| **Germanene** | ≈ 25 meV (≈ 290 K) | DFT–PBE + SOC (e.g., Ezawa, PRB 2012) |
| **Stanene** | ≈ 0.10 eV (≈ 1160 K) | DFT–HSE06 + SOC (e.g., Xu *et al.*, Nat. Commun. 2014) |
| **Plumbene** | ≈ 0.40 eV (≈ 4640 K) | DFT–PBE + SOC (e.g., Liu *et al.*, J. Phys.: Condens. Matter 2021) |

> **Key points**
> 
> 1. The QSH phase in these Xenes is driven by strong intrinsic spin‑orbit coupling (SOC).  
> 2. The band gaps quoted above are the *direct* SOC‑induced gaps at the Dirac‑like K/K′ points; they determine the temperature range over which edge states can be observed without thermal activation of bulk carriers.  
> 3. Experimental confirmation has been achieved for **stanene** on Bi₂Te₃ (ARPES) and for **plumbene** on Ag(111) (STM/STS), while silicene and germanene remain in the *predicted* regime, with ongoing efforts to stabilize them on insulating substrates.

Thus, among the family of two‑dimensional “Xenes”, silicene, germanene, stanene, and plumbene are the ones that have been predicted—by first‑principles calculations—to be quantum spin Hall insulators.

Bei sehr niedrigen Temperaturen (typischerweise unter etwa 180 K) tritt in 1T‑TaS₂ die **kommensurierte Charge‑Density‑Wave‑Phase** (C‑Phase) auf. In dieser Phase bildet sich ein \(3\times3\)‑Superlattice aus Ta‑Atomen, das zu einer „Star‑of‑David“‑Struktur führt und die elektronische Bandstruktur stark verändert – etwa durch Öffnen eines pseudogap‑ähnlichen Bereichs bei der Fermi‑Ebene. Diese Phase ist die stabile Grundphase des Materials im Low‑Temperature‑Bereich.

Graphenylene forms a two‑dimensional carbon network that follows the **Archimedean tiling (4, 8²)** – i.e., a pattern of alternating squares and octagons. In this lattice each vertex is surrounded by one square (four‑membered ring) and two octagons (eight‑membered rings), giving the characteristic “square–octagon” motif that defines graphenylene.
